steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on solving Raven Progressive Matrices with deep learning. Explain what RPM tasks are and why they matter for AI, describe the biased answer set problem in existing datasets like RAVEN, and introduce our two-stage approach and transformer model, ending with the list of contributions.

Abstract reasoning is one of the key attributes of general intelligence, and among other things it includes the capacity to reason about sequential patterns and complete them. John C. Raven devised a visual test in the 1930s to quantify this capability in humans and to diagnose deficiencies related to it, and this test is now known as Raven Progressive Matrices (RPM). An RPM problem (Fig. 1) is a 3x3 grid with eight context panels that contain arrangements of 2D geometric objects. The objects follow rules that govern how the panels in a row relate to each other, for example a progression of the number of objects, or a logical operation about whether they are present, etc. The task is to complete the puzzle by replacing the query panel in the lower right with the correct image, chosen from eight answer panels. To solve it one has to 'disentangle' the rules for the rows and columns and capture the analogies between the patterns that are observed.

More recently RPMs have been adopted in the AI community to assess similar capabilities in artificial intelligent systems, together with other benchmarks like Bongard problems and Hofstadter's analogies. Recent advances in machine learning accelerated this trend, and deep learning became the primary paradigm of choice for designing such systems.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Abstract reasoning is one of the key attributes of general intelligence, and among other things it includes the capacity to reason about sequential patterns and complete them. John C. Raven devised a visual test in the 1930s to quantify this capability in humans and to diagnose deficiencies related to it, and this test is now known as Raven Progressive Matrices (RPM). An RPM problem (Fig. 1) is a 3x3 grid with eight context panels that contain arrangements of 2D geometric objects. The objects follow rules that govern how the panels in a row relate to each other, for example a progression of the number of objects, or a logical operation about whether they are present, etc. The task is to complete the puzzle by replacing the query panel in the lower right with the correct image, chosen from eight answer panels. To solve it one has to 'disentangle' the rules for the rows and columns and capture the analogies between the patterns that are observed.

More recently RPMs have been adopted in the AI community to assess similar capabilities in artificial intelligent systems, together with other benchmarks like Bongard problems and Hofstadter's analogies. Recent advances in machine learning accelerated this trend, and deep learning became the primary paradigm of choice for designing such systems.

The original collection of RPM problems, the Standard Progressive Matrices, had just 60 tasks, and this is not enough to train data-hungry machine learning models well. So several larger datasets and task generators were made, for example RAVEN and I-RAVEN. While doing this it became clear that it is nontrivial to design a collection of RPM tasks that is representative, diverse and varying in difficulty. The main challenge is that you need to generate 7 incorrect answer panels in such a way that the correct answer panel cannot be deduced from them. Most tasks in RAVEN do not meet this requirement, unfortunately. The correct answer panel can be selected by finding the most frequent attributes (shape, size, etc.) across all 8 answer panels and then picking the answer panel that has those properties. This flaw is easy to exploit, and so-called context-blind methods did exactly that: they get almost perfect scores on RAVEN while disregarding the context completely and deciding only based on the answer panels. This problem has been called biased answer set, and we illustrate it in Sec. SM9 of the Supplementary Material (SM).

In this study we get around this problem by decomposing RPM tasks into two stages: 1) predicting properties of the query panel, and 2) identifying the answer panel whose properties match the predicted ones the most. For this we use the abstract properties that are available in RAVEN benchmarks, and we design a bespoke deep learning architecture which is based on the transformer blueprint. We call the resulting approach Abstract Compositional Transformer. It is more transparent than end-to-end neural architectures, it is also immune to biased answer sets, and it can surpass the state-of-the-art performance. The property prediction stage is immune to biases since it does not involve the answer panels, and the second stage does not involve learning, so by definition it cannot be biased by what is in a training set. Also, to the best knowledge of the authors, this is the first attempt to predict symbolic descriptors of RPM puzzles, and the first study on self-supervised learning for RPM. Our main contributions are the two-stage approach and model architecture (Sec. 2), a bespoke training procedure (Sec. 3) and an extensive empirical analysis about property prediction (Sec. 5) and problem solving (Sec. 6).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
One of the key attributes of general intelligence is abstract reasoning, which, among others, includes the capacity to reason about and complete sequential patterns. To quantify such capabilities in humans and diagnose related deficiencies, John C. Raven devised in the 1930s a visual test now known as Raven Progressive Matrices (RPM) [1]. An RPM problem (Fig. 1) is a 3x3 grid of eight context panels containing arrangements of 2D geometric objects. The objects follow rules that govern the relationships between the panels in rows, e.g. progression of the number of objects, a logical operation concerning their presence, etc. The task is to complete the puzzle by replacing the lower-right query panel with the correct image from the eight provided answer panels. Solving the task requires 'disentangling' the rules corresponding to rows and columns and capturing the analogies between the observed patterns.

RPMs have more recently been adopted in the AI community for assessing similar capabilities in artificial intelligent systems, along with other benchmarks like Bongard problems [2] and Hofstadter's analogies [3]. Recent advances in machine learning accelerated this trend, with deep learning becoming the primary paradigm of choice for designing such systems [4].

The original collection of RPM problems, Standard Progressive Matrices [1], comprised just 60 tasks, which is not enough to effectively train data-hungry machine learning models. Therefore, several larger datasets and task generators have been devised, among them RAVEN [5] and I-RAVEN [6]. In this process, it became evident that designing a representative, diverse, and varying in difficulty collection of RPM tasks is nontrivial. The key challenge is that one needs to generate 7 incorrect answer panels such that the correct answer panel cannot be deduced from them. Unfortunately, most tasks in RAVEN do not meet this requirement: the correct answer panel can be selected by identifying the most frequent attributes across all 8 answer panels (shape, size, etc.) and picking the answer panel with those properties. This flaw can be easily exploited, as shown by so-called context-blind methods [7] that achieve almost perfect scores on RAVEN by disregarding the context entirely and deciding based on answer panels only. This problem has been termed biased answer set, and we illustrate it in Sec. SM9 of the Supplementary Material (SM).

In this study, we circumvent this problem by decomposing RPM tasks into two stages: 1) prediction of properties of the query panel, and 2) identifying the answer panel with properties that best match the predicted ones. To this aim, we use the abstract properties available in RAVEN benchmarks and design a bespoke deep learning architecture based on the transformer blueprint [8]. The resulting approach, which we call Abstract Compositional Transformer, is more transparent than end-to-end neural architectures, immune to biased answer sets and capable of surpassing the state-of-the-art performance. More specifically, the property prediction stage is immune to biases because it does not involve the answer panels, while the second stage does not involve learning and thus by definition cannot be biased by the content of a training set. Also, to the best knowledge of the authors, this is the first attempt to predict symbolic descriptors of RPM puzzles and the first study on self-supervised learning for RPM. Our main contributions are the two-stage approach and model architecture (Sec. 2), a bespoke training procedure (Sec. 3) and an extensive empirical analysis concerning property prediction (Sec. 5) and problem solving (Sec. 6).

References:

[2] M.M. Bongard. Pattern recognition. 1970.
[3] Douglas R. Hofstadter. Fluid concepts & creative analogies : computer models of the fundamental mechanisms of thought . Basic Books, New York, 1995.
